title: A Dry Look at Toilet Paper
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and manufacture of toilet paper, from ancient wiping materials and Joseph Gayetty's medicated paper sheets, through the Scott brothers' first roll and the Sharmin brand with Mr. Whipple, to the 1973 Johnny Carson toilet paper shortage joke. They cover how toilet paper is made (pulp, bleaching, sheeting, cardboard tubes, plies, recycled paper), colored toilet paper, over/underhang debate, and the environmental cost compared with bidets and wet wipes. Also includes tour announcements, a groom of the stool correction, and a listener mail about gender-neutral pronouns and the term cisgender.
topics: over or under toilet paper roll

segments.title: Tour announcement and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh announces 2017 tour dates and cities, then Josh and Chuck introduce the toilet paper episode, noting Americans' heavy toilet paper use and their opinions on wiping with water.

segments.title: Bidets and personal toilet paper habits
segments.summary: The hosts discuss their own bidets and Japanese toilet seats with built-in bidets, and joke about the George Carlin bit on sitting on the toilet.

segments.title: Ancient wiping materials and royal grooms of the stool
segments.summary: Historical wiping materials are covered, including leaves, moss, shells, corn cobs, sheep's wool, and lace. Josh corrects his misreading of the groom of the stool role, which involved commode upkeep rather than wiping. Ancient Greek and Roman methods, including the ostracon, are also covered.

segments.title: Joseph Gayetty's medicated paper and early American use
segments.summary: In 1857 New York, Joseph Gayetty sold medicated paper sheets marketed for hemorrhoids. Sales were slow because Americans used the Farmer's Almanac and Sears catalog, and people did not want to discuss the topic.
topics: Farmer's Almanac and Sears catalog as toilet paper

segments.title: Scott brothers, roll invention, and Sharmin marketing
segments.summary: Clarence and Irvin Scott created the first toilet paper on a roll, released under shame-avoiding branding until 1902. Three changes (indoor plumbing, slick Sears catalog paper, and Hoberg Paper's Sharmin brand) helped toilet paper become mainstream. Dick Wilson played Mr. Whipple in Sharmin ads.

segments.title: Johnny Carson joke and the 1973 toilet paper shortage
segments.summary: Johnny Carson joked on The Tonight Show about a toilet paper shortage in 1973, and viewers hoarded the product, creating a real shortage for weeks in some places.

segments.title: Toilet paper as a marker of national development
segments.summary: Mental Floss article notes toilet paper purchases rise as countries become more sanitary and prosperous. Brazil has doubled its sales since 2004 while American sales have plateaued. Many places still use water or buckets.

segments.title: How toilet paper is manufactured
segments.summary: Trees are chipped, cooked in a digester into pulp, bleached, mixed with water, pressed onto screens and dried. Cardboard tubes are formed, glued, and cut into rolls. Recycled paper undergoes de-inking with foam flotation. Plies and embossing add softness and strength.

segments.title: Colored toilet paper and dyes
segments.summary: Colored toilet paper was popular in the 1970s to match bathroom decor. Dyes were dropped over health concerns and cost. Renova still sells colored toilet paper.

segments.title: Over or under hang debate and toilet paper origami
segments.summary: The hosts debate over versus underhang orientation, citing a Simpsons joke, Seth Wheeler's perforated roll patent, and kid and dog-proofing. They discuss wall-mounted holders and knuckle contact, and mention a toilet paper origami book.

segments.title: Bidets, wipes, and environmental cost
segments.summary: The hosts compare bidet water use with toilet paper's cost in water, electricity, trees and wood. They discuss flushable wipes not breaking down, a Consumer Reports test, and the risks of wipes for irritation.

segments.title: Lota, shrinking rolls, and wrap-up
segments.summary: Hosts mention the lota used by Muslims for cleansing and a Vice article on it. They also note toilet paper rolls have gotten narrower and shorter while prices rise, and wrap up the segment.

segments.title: Listener mail on pronouns and cisgender
segments.summary: Listener Chase corrects the hosts on the term cisgender and suggests they, them as a singular pronoun. Hosts thank Chase and comment on LGBTQIA alphabet soup.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact information
segments.summary: Hosts give social media, email, and website contact information and sign off.
